title: What is an Object? (Instances in Heap)
summary: Step into RAM: see how objects are born on the Heap while reference variables live on the Stack.
learningObjectives: Differentiate the class blueprint from a runtime object instance
Understand the 'new' keyword and dynamic Heap memory allocation
Explain how object references on the Stack point to memory addresses on the Heap
Answer technical interview questions on object creation and garbage collection
expectedOutcomes: Confidence creating multiple objects from a class and tracing their independent state

analogy.headline: Why do we need objects if we already wrote the class?
analogy.story: An architectural blueprint for a 3-bedroom house is not a house: you cannot sleep in a blueprint, park your car in it, or paint its walls. The blueprint (Class) only describes the layout. When the construction crew actually builds houses in the physical neighborhood (Heap memory), each built house is an Object. House 101 can be painted blue, while House 102 can be painted yellow. They share the same blueprint, but maintain completely independent physical state.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A Class is a template in bytecode. An Object is an actual runtime instance living in computer memory (Heap) with its own state.

activities.title: Memory Architecture: Stack vs Heap
activities.content:
When you execute:
`Car myCar = new Car();`

Two distinct memory operations happen simultaneously:
1. **`Car myCar` (Stack)**: A reference variable named `myCar` is created on the current method's Stack frame. It does NOT store the car itself; it holds a 64-bit memory address pointer.
2. **`new Car()` (Heap)**: The `new` keyword dynamically allocates a block of memory on the Heap for the car's fields (color, speed, fuel) and calls the constructor.
3. **`=` (Assignment)**: The reference variable on the Stack is assigned the address of the newly constructed Heap object.

activities.title: Creating Independent Objects
activities.description: Notice: accelerating `car1` altered only `car1.speed`. `car2.speed` remains 0 because both cars occupy completely distinct addresses in Heap memory.

questions.prompt: Consider: Car a = new Car(); Car b = a; b.speed = 50; What is the value of a.speed?
options: 50 (both variables point to the same Heap object)

hints.hint: Did the 'new' keyword get called a second time?
'Car b = a' copies the memory address from 'a' into 'b'.

questions.explanation: Because 'new Car()' was only executed once, only ONE object exists on the Heap. Both 'a' and 'b' on the Stack hold the exact same memory address. Mutating through 'b' affects the object viewed by 'a'.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between an Object and an Object Reference?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Think of an object as a house, and a reference as a slip of paper with that house's address written on it. The object holds the real data in memory, while the reference is just the variable that tells Java where to find it.
keyPoints: The object holds actual data; the reference holds its memory location
Multiple references can point to the same single object

activities.title: Mastery Verification Checklist
checklist: I can explain the difference between a class and an object using real-world analogies.
I can draw the Stack and Heap memory diagram for 'Car c = new Car()'.
I understand what happens when two references point to the same object.
